items.reason: No aired line says it or works this way. Looked at hard and passed: the previous aired episode's song turned on the host having exactly one small thing to offer (one note) after saying he only hosts, and the record says a joke whose punch is that he is only a host, a mouth or a throat has been made. This is not that joke. The line is a set-up and not a punch, it does not name his job or his size, and the 'one line' is his company on the block, not his shortfall; it mends 'on my own' in the line before it. The pilot's 'exactly one setting' was a joke about a bot's tic. What the line adds to the shape of the ending is a different matter, set out under earnsItsPlace and forTheOwner; it does not make the line a repeat.

An exact line of a published translation that the show has never said, and no aired episode has had a house character recite an old text at all. The nearest thing in the record is the pilot's sincere beat, which let other people's words (real posts held on cards) say what the night was about and then undercut it with a sound from the audience. Different mechanism: here one man says one line by heart to the road, nothing is put on screen, and what follows is his own flinch and not an interruption. Borrowed words and lightness within a beat are the premise chapter's craft for sincerity, not a device of an episode. Both reviewers read these same words against the same aired record at select and neither stopped them.

Looked at hardest of the four. Twice last week Larry ended a sincere passage by saying the thing was not really his: at the bottom of the making-of, after telling the viewer they make the show, he was only a mouth; in the song, asked for his best, he only hosted. One sentence can be stretched over all three (after something sincere, the host says it is not his). I pass it because the punch is different in kind: those two were about how small his part in the show is, and the record lists that joke as made. This one is a man embarrassed at having been overheard meaning something, blaming the book; it says nothing about the show or his job, and the next beat takes it half back, which neither earlier line did. It is the character (ducks credit at the tender moment) with a new line, which the record allows. No aired line uses the words.

Never said on air. The form, a flat statement and then a one- or two-word qualifier as its own beat, has one near relative in the previous aired episode (a claim that nothing gets in twice, then a dry exception). There the qualifier was the joke, about the show's own process; here it is a man giving back half of what he has just disowned, and it is the truest word in the moment. Ordinary speech, different job. It also belongs to this script's own Larry, who answered 'Does it help?' with 'Some nights.'

joins: The moment still does what I praised it for at select, and does it better here. Then it was the one place he said he was glad of us, in a line that is not his, to the road, with the feeling carried by where his head points and half taken back. All of that is intact (`comrade-line` said ahead, the cue `glance`, `poem-talking`, `mostly`), and three changes help it. The poem's own lead-in is gone, so the 'alone' the line answers is now Larry's (`this-block`) and not a speaker's in a book; nothing is introduced with 'There's ...', so it does not arrive as a third lesson; and the poem's name has gone to the credits, which takes a hard word out of the tenderest ten seconds. It also has more under it than in the draft it came from: the unheard answer, 'I don't know', the red light and five seconds of snow. And it puts back what I said in round 1 had gone with the cut. Two more gains further on. 'I had company.' (`company`) is no longer the first time he says it; it is now the plain version, said to his friends, of what he took half back on the street, and it lands as the end of that. And the stretch I flagged in round 1 as about 85 seconds without one light line now has one at its middle. The couplet at the door: two jobs, not the same thing twice, but one shape twice. The Norse line is a feeling about the walk that is ending, said to nobody and then disowned; the Tamil couplet is an obligation about the meal that is starting, said up at a window and then pleaded ('So you see my position.'). He pushes the first book away and hides behind the second, and that is one man. The second gains a joke from the first: by `q-come-up` we already know what he wants, so reaching for another old book instead of answering is funnier than it was. It also loses something. In round 1 the door was where we learned he wanted us there (the cue `back-to-us` has him 'caught wanting us to come'); he has now been caught once already, half a minute earlier, so the door is less a discovery and more a man failing to say what we know. And the shape repeats closely: an old text, a line of it, a look at us with a tilt, a dry line. Three things show at the joins. (1) 'old': `old-books`, 'an old Chinese book', 'an old Norse poem', and about twenty-five seconds later 'There's an old Tamil book of couplets called the Tirukkural'. My round 1 note that `tamil-book` announces itself as another book is stronger now that it is the fourth of the night and the second on this street. (2) Larry alone: 'on my own' (`this-block`), 'Just me' (`one-line`) and 'They'll have started without me.' (`started-without-me`) are three lines inside about forty seconds that say he is by himself or expects to be. Dry, each is fine; together they lean toward a man sorry for himself, which he is not. (3) He now quotes himself habitually at both ends of the walk: a sentence he keeps saying (`cant-believe`) and a line he walks with (`one-line`). That one I think is a rhyme and not a fault: all he has of his own at the start, something better borrowed by the end. Nothing in the new lines uses the door's words or the table's. Housekeeping the writer has already named: the footsteps under the block are about twelve seconds short, the comment at the top of the script still says three ideas and one translation, and `notes.json` is out of date. 438 words by the round 1 count, inside the range.
earnsItsPlace: Yes, the fourth earns its place, because it is not a fourth lesson. The cook and the rabbi are things offered to the viewer about carrying on; the Norse line offers nothing and explains nothing, and is the hinge where the special turns from carrying on to company, which is what the door, the table and the owner's last lines are about. That subject had one text and now has two, as the first has two. It makes us want to come up before anyone asks, it gives the heaviest stretch its one light beat, and it lets `company` finish something. What it costs is paid at the door and at the kerb, not on the block: the couplet becomes the second old text in half a minute and loses its surprise, and the rabbi's sentence, which is the idea the special exists for, is now followed forty seconds later by a second quotation in old English that is shorter, warmer and easier to keep. If something is now one too many it is an introduction and not an idea: the sentence that brings in the Tamil book. On the close: it does not change the mechanism I passed in round 1, and it does add the one step of the two aired song endings that this ending did not have. Both of those began with the host alone and unsure, offering one small thing of his own, before a flat line took him in and the room came up. This ending now also begins with Larry alone on his block with one line, saying it and backing away from it. With `started-without-me` and the kept chair, the last ninety seconds are now as much about Larry turning out to be less alone than he thinks as about us being let in. I still judge it a different thing: nobody answers or makes good his one line, a whole scene stands between it and the table, nothing is sung or lit for him, and the one a chair is made for is the viewer. But it is nearer the earlier two closes than it was this morning, and the owner should hear that from someone with the record.
forTheOwner: From the record, for you and not for a writer. In round 1 I told you this is the third close of three in which someone is taken in, and that the look, the flat line and the place made at the table follow last week's song step for step. The Norse line adds the step that was missing: both aired songs began their endings with Larry alone and unsure, offering one small thing of his own. He now does that on the last block. I pass all four lines, and I think the moment is the best thing in the last two minutes; you kept last week's ending knowing what it repeated, and you should keep this one knowing the same.

`started-without-me` again. You left it as written. It now follows 'on my own' and 'Just me' by a few seconds, so it is the third line in forty seconds that has him by himself, and with the Norse line before it the table is more plainly about him being waited for. The choice I put to you in round 1 is weightier than it was; it is still yours and could still go either way.

The door. The couplet is now the second old text in half a minute and the fourth of the night, and its first sentence is the longest introduction of the four, with the hardest name, where a viewer is waiting to be asked in. The assembly's 'not both' was about this. I think both can stand because the second is played as a dodge and gains a laugh from the first; the door does lose its surprise.

Which sentence a viewer leaves with. There are now two exact quotations in old English forty seconds apart. The rabbi's is the one your outline's first half is about (keep going); the Norse one is the one your last lines are about (keep them close), and it is the easier to remember. If the measure is what people say Larry told them, expect the answer to move toward company.
Names. The Norse poem is not named aloud and loses nothing by it; the Chinese and Tamil books still are. That is one more piece of evidence for the either-or on names that the assembly put to you.

Length. Your outline aimed at four minutes; this adds about twelve seconds to a cut already past that, and the new seconds are in the back half, where three of the four texts now fall inside about a minute and a half.

Not heard by me. `comrade-line` has its words out of their usual order and wants to be heard once to know that it parses; 'Mostly.' is one word standing as its own beat, which the writer says may have to rejoin the line before it; and the glance has to read as a man who has just heard himself, which is staging's.
